answers.ease: Honestly, the sign-in and workspace setup looks simpler than what we deal with in Veeva Vault — one card, clear buttons, and the MFA enrollment steps are spelled out. For me and my team of nine, I don't see anyone struggling here, even the folks who grumble about new software. My only friction point would be the password reset requiring you to sign out first — that's an extra step people will forget.
answers.clarity: The language is plain and I appreciate that — "one workspace per client company" maps exactly to how a CRO like ours thinks about client isolation. The helper text on passwords and MFA codes is clearer than most enterprise tools I've bought. The one term that gave me pause is "dossier manager" versus "Portfolio" versus "Registry" in the top bar — I'd want to know which one holds my actual sequences before I click around.
answers.trust: For a real ANDS filing, sign-in is table stakes, but the details here matter to me and most of them check out: per-workspace isolation enforced at the API, append-only audit trail, salted hashes, self-hosted with data staying in our environment — those are exactly the questions our clients' quality auditors ask. What stops me is no SAML/OIDC yet; our IT will not approve a team rollout without SSO, full stop. And the demo showing the reset code on-screen made me wince until I read the production caveat — I'd want that verified in writing.
answers.feedback: I genuinely like the "Deployment & data residency" card — after 22 years I've never seen a vendor state "cross-workspace reads are refused at the API, not just hidden in the UI" that plainly, and I'd quote it to clients. I also like that MFA setup tells you nothing is enforced until the code verifies, so nobody locks themselves out. What I'd change: add SSO before asking a 400-person CRO to adopt this, let users change passwords while signed in instead of routing through "Forgot password?", and clarify the difference between Portfolio and Registry right on the landing page. One more: 12-hour sessions feel long for a system holding client dossiers — I'd want that configurable.

answers.ease: Honestly, a login screen is a login screen — my team could handle this without training, which is more than I can say for the first week of Veeva. The MFA enrollment with the copy-link option and the "nothing is enforced until this code verifies" note is sensible; I've watched people lock themselves out of systems mid-filing and this avoids that.
answers.clarity: The language is plain and I appreciate that "one workspace per client company" is spelled out twice — as a CRO that's exactly the question I'd ask first. The one thing that gave me pause is "New client? Create a workspace" — in my world "client" means the sponsor, so I'd want to be sure it's the CRO admin creating workspaces on their behalf, not the sponsor self-registering.
answers.trust: For sign-in itself, mostly yes — self-hosted, HttpOnly sessions, append-only audit trail, and API-level workspace isolation are the right answers for what our clients' security questionnaires ask. But no SSO is a real problem: our IT will not approve a new system holding client dossiers without SAML, and I'd also want the demo one-time-code-on-screen behaviour certified as off in production, not just promised in a notice box.
answers.feedback: I like the honesty — the demo-mode disclosure, the plain statement of password hashing and session length, and the data-residency card are things I usually have to drag out of vendors through a 40-question form. Concretely I would change three things: ship SSO before asking a 400-person CRO to manage passwords; add role-based access detail on the Account page (I have 9 people who need different permissions per client, and "your role" as a single line tells me nothing); and rename "New client? Create a workspace" to something like "Set up a client workspace" so nobody thinks sponsors sign themselves up.

answers.ease: Honestly, this looks easier than what my team deals with in docuBridge day to day. The 10-step rail with plain-language lock reasons is the kind of hand-holding I wish Veeva had for junior associates. My only worry is the "3D tower" of module tiles — I don't need decoration, I need to see gaps, and flashy visuals tend to slow older machines and older eyes like mine.
answers.clarity: The terminology is largely correct — Dossier ID format (letter plus 6-7 digits), Company ID enrolment via the OSIP-BPIP mailbox, the three-receipt sequence through the FDA gateway — that's real Health Canada process, and whoever wrote this has actually filed. "Readiness: BLOCKED" and "the single thing standing between you and ready" is refreshingly plain. The one thing I'd tighten is the "new use the brand isn't approved for" checkbox — that's flirting with 505(b)(2)-style territory that doesn't map cleanly to an ANDS, and it needs more explanation than a checkbox.
answers.trust: Not on a walkthrough alone — I file on behalf of clients, and one rejected sequence costs me a relationship. That said, the details give me more confidence than most vendor demos: correct MDN/ACK/Core ID receipt order, the two-week Company ID enrolment reality, gated continuation until Module 1-5 documents are placed. I'd trust it after running a parallel dry-run against a sequence we've already filed through docuBridge, and after seeing its validation catch the errors the CESG catches.
answers.feedback: I like the "I've requested it — continue while it's pending" control for Company ID — that's exactly how real timelines work, and blocking there would be dilettante software. I like the disabled Continue with a plain reason instead of a cryptic error. What I'd change: give me a multi-dossier team view up front — I manage 9 people and dozens of concurrent sequences, and this reads like it's built for one person filing one product. And "Start over" in the top bar makes me nervous; if someone on my team clicks that on a 70%-ready dossier, I need to know it's recoverable.

answers.ease: For me personally, the step-by-step rail with plain-language explanations reads as very manageable — honestly easier than the first week I spent learning Vault RIM. My concern is my team of nine: a 10-step wizard is fine for one product, but we run dozens of sequences in parallel, so I'd want to know how this scales beyond the "hold my hand" mode before I'd call it easy in practice.
answers.clarity: The vocabulary is right — Dossier ID format, Company ID, eCTD Modules 1–5, the three receipts in order — that's exactly how OSIP actually works, and the lock reasons on future steps are a nice touch. The one thing I'd flag is "riding the US FDA gateway" — I know it's the CESG arrangement, but a junior associate or a client reading over our shoulder will be confused why the FDA appears in a Canadian filing; that needs a fuller explanation right there.
answers.trust: Partial trust. The enrolment realities are correct — the Company Template email to hc.osip-bpip.sc@canada.ca and the weeks of waiting, the e123456 dossier format, the MDN/ACK/Core ID sequence — someone who has actually filed built this. But I am accountable for client filings, and a "READY TO FILE" badge from a wizard is not a substitute for my QA lead's review or LORENZ validation; I'd rely on it for orchestration and tracking, not as the final word before transmission.
answers.feedback: I genuinely like the "single thing standing between you and ready" resume line — that is exactly what my Excel trackers try and fail to do — and the "continue while it's pending" control for Company ID enrolment shows real process knowledge. I dislike the 3D tower; it looks like decoration where I want a dense module completeness table. I'd also want the validation step to name which validator ruleset it runs (Health Canada eCTD validation rules, version number), an audit trail behind the e-signature step, and multi-user visibility so I can see where each of my nine associates' dossiers sits without opening them one by one.

answers.ease: Honestly, this looks straightforward enough — two fields to create a dossier is far simpler than setting up a binder in Veeva, and the placeholder-ID option would let my team start work before Health Canada issues the ID, which is how projects actually run. My only worry is training nine people on yet another tool, but there's not much here to trip on. I'd want to see how it behaves with forty-plus active dossiers, though — a grid of tiles gets unwieldy fast.
answers.clarity: The explanatory text is better than most vendors manage — spelling out that the Dossier ID comes from a Dossier ID Request through REP via CESG tells me whoever wrote this actually knows the Health Canada process, which is rare. The ID format validation with the e123456 example is exactly right. The one thing that would confuse my juniors is the "CS-BE" tag on every tile with no explanation — I know what it means, but a new RA associate wouldn't, and not every ANDS is a CS-BE pathway anyway.
answers.trust: Partly. The workspace isolation statement matters to me since we handle multiple clients, and the promise that documents, sequences and history all move when a placeholder ID is replaced is critical — but I'd need that demonstrated and documented before trusting it, because a broken ID migration on a live file would be a disaster. What genuinely alarms me is a plain "✕" delete that permanently destroys a dossier and all its documents behind a native browser confirm — in Veeva nothing is truly deleted, and for regulated records I need an audit trail and soft-delete, not "this cannot be undone".
answers.feedback: I like the placeholder-ID workflow, the accurate REP/CESG guidance, and the module-count status chips — that at-a-glance readiness view beats my Excel tracker. I dislike the browser prompt/confirm dialogs for renaming and deleting; that reads as unfinished and would not pass our vendor qualification, so replace them with proper in-app modals requiring a typed confirmation. Add a tooltip or make CS-BE configurable per dossier, remove permanent deletion in favor of archive-with-audit-trail, and give me a list view with sorting and filtering by client and deadline — tiles alone won't scale for a CRO portfolio.

answers.ease: For me personally, creating a dossier looks simple enough — two fields and a button is not going to trip up anyone on my team. What gives me pause is the little things: renaming a Dossier ID through a browser prompt box is the kind of clunky interaction I'd expect from an internal IT tool, not something I'd roll out to nine people managing client filings.
answers.clarity: The terminology is actually correct, which I appreciate — they know the Dossier ID comes from a Dossier ID Request through REP via CESG, and the format hint "one letter + 6–7 digits" matches reality. I'd want "CS-BE" explained on the tile though; I know what it means, but my newer associates would be googling it.
answers.trust: Partially. The workspace isolation statement matters to me because we handle multiple sponsors, but a claim in a paragraph is not an audit — I'd need our IT and QA to verify it before any client data goes in. And a delete button that permanently destroys a dossier and all documents behind a single native confirm dialog is frankly alarming; in Veeva nothing is ever truly deleted, and Health Canada expects a full audit trail. That alone would keep this out of production use for us.
answers.feedback: I genuinely like the placeholder-ID flow — teams do start building before REP issues the ID, and "validation reminds you before filing" is how it should work; the draft IDs starting with "d" so nobody mistakes them for real ones is a thoughtful touch. What I'd change: replace the browser prompt/confirm dialogs with proper in-app modals with an audit record; make delete a soft archive with recovery, or restrict it by role; and show who created and last modified each dossier on the tile — accountability across a team of nine is not optional for me.

answers.ease: On paper it looks manageable — the three-column layout with a section tree and status glyphs is familiar territory from LORENZ, and the tabs for Upload versus Author in-app are self-explanatory. My worry is the density: circles, half-circles, checkmarks, chips, readiness flags, provenance tags all at once would overwhelm my newer associates on day one. I'd want a proper training session before rolling this out to a team of nine.
answers.clarity: The regulatory vocabulary is genuinely correct — "Canadian Reference Product (brand)", "s.5 statement (per patent)", AUC 90% CI — which tells me someone who has actually filed an ANDS wrote these labels. The "What Health Canada needs here" teach box with a guidance link is exactly what I wish Vault had. The one thing I'd flag: "Author" as a verb on a button is a bit precious — my staff would ask whether it generates a document or just saves the form.
answers.trust: Not without knowing what "Health Canada review: no blocking content gaps" is actually checking against — is it the current guidance version, and who maintains those rules when Health Canada updates them? I've been burned by tools whose validation lagged a guidance revision by a year. The provenance chips, md5 fragments, and the explicit "AI-assisted — review before filing" warning are the right instincts and I'd trust it as a drafting and completeness aid, but final sign-off stays with my reviewers, full stop.
answers.feedback: I like the "Not required for this generic (N)" collapsed list — knowing what you can skip is half the battle in an ANDS — and the sample pre-fill with visible "sample" tags is smart, provided every last tag clears before filing. What I'd change: I need a hard block, not a note, if any "sample" field survives to export — a worked example slipping into a real 1.2.5 would be a catastrophic client conversation. I'd also want the review findings exportable so I can attach them to our internal QC record, and a visible date/version stamp on the Health Canada rules being checked.

answers.ease: For me personally, the three-column layout with the section tree and status glyphs is close enough to how docuBridge organizes an eCTD backbone that I could find my way around. My worry is my more junior associates confusing the "sample" pre-filled fields with real data — pre-fill is convenient, but a hurried person under a client deadline will leave a worked example in a filing field. The Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A choice is simple enough that I would not need training for the basics.
answers.clarity: The vocabulary is genuinely correct for once — "Canadian Reference Product (brand)", "s.5 statement (per patent)", "AUC 90% CI" tells me someone who has actually read the Patented Medicines regulations wrote this, not just a software team. The "What Health Canada needs here" teach box with a link to the actual guidance is exactly what I make my team keep in a binder today. What is not clear to me is what "Health Canada review" means — is this checking against Health Canada's actual validation rules, or the vendor's interpretation of them? That distinction matters enormously and the label blurs it.
answers.trust: Not without knowing what sits behind "Health Canada review: no blocking content gaps" — I have been burned by vendor validators that pass a sequence Health Canada then screens out. The provenance chips (authored in-app, uploaded, "AI-assisted — review before filing") and the md5 fragment are the right instincts and I would cite them to a client auditor, but I would still run every output through LORENZ validation and my own checklist before anything goes to the Minister. The "AI-assisted" flag would earn cautious trust, not blind trust.
answers.feedback: I like the provenance chips, the readiness flags on the right rail, and the "Not required for this generic" collapsed list — knowing what you do NOT need to file is half the battle in an ANDS. Concretely: the sample pre-fill needs a hard gate — the system should refuse to mark a section complete while any "sample" tag remains, otherwise a placeholder will end up in a real submission on my watch. Rename "Health Canada review" to something honest like "Pre-validation check against HC guidance" and state which guidance version and date it checks against. And the placeholder Dossier ID path needs a visible reminder trail — I have seen sequences rejected over an identifier nobody went back to correct.
answers.adoption: I would pilot it on one internal dossier alongside our current Veeva/LORENZ workflow before letting client work near it, and I would want the validation-rule sourcing documented in writing first.

answers.ease: For me personally, the chat itself looks manageable — type what you know, press Send, review the draft. But I worry about my team of nine treating this like a shortcut; the fact that the "review vs Health Canada" step lives under a separate mode you have to go hunting for means the easy path is draft-and-save without the check. Easy to use is not the same as easy to use correctly.
answers.clarity: Most of the labels are clear enough — "req/opt", the AI badge tooltip, "Nothing is saved until you click Use this draft" is exactly the reassurance I'd want spelled out. But "Sample & edit" as the home of both the standard Author function and the compliance review is confusing, and the error message pointing to an "Author button below" that isn't actually below would send my juniors in circles.
answers.trust: Not without changes. I like that provenance is recorded in the audit trail and the "AI-assisted — review before filing" chip stays on the document — that's the right instinct, and it's what I'd need to defend to a client or during a Health Canada screening deficiency. But burying the confirmation and the review instruction in a screen-reader-only region is unacceptable for accountability; if my reviewer never sees the prompt to check against guidance, that draft goes into a sequence unverified under my name.
answers.feedback: Keep: the audit-trail provenance, the persistent AI-assisted chip, the explicit "nothing saved until you approve" language, and the AI asking for details instead of leaving blanks — blank placeholders are how deficiencies happen. Change: make the save confirmation and the "Review vs Health Canada" instruction visible on screen for everyone, ideally as a required review step or at least a prominent banner, not a hidden live region. Fix the misconfigured-AI error to say exactly where the Author option lives. And I'd want a way to see, at the dossier level, which documents are AI-drafted and still unreviewed — as the person signing off on client filings, I need that list, not a per-document chip.

answers.ease: The chat itself looks easy enough — even my most junior associate types into boxes all day. But easy in the wrong way worries me: after 22 years I know the hard part isn't producing text, it's producing the right text, and this puts drafting one Enter key away from anyone on my team of nine. I'd also need to hunt around modes to find things — the review step and the fallback "Author" button apparently live somewhere other than where the system tells you to look.
answers.clarity: The section panel is well laid out — "What Health Canada needs here" with a guidance link is exactly how I train my people, and the req/opt badges are sensible. But "Draft with AI" versus "Sample & edit" is muddy — which one is authoring, and why is "Review vs Health Canada" buried under Sample & edit? And a save confirmation that only exists in a screen-reader region is not a confirmation; my staff will save a draft and have no visible instruction that a review step even exists.
answers.trust: Not without controls I don't see here. I like that provenance is logged and the "AI-assisted — review before filing" chip exists, but a chip is not a workflow — in Veeva I can enforce a review-and-approve lifecycle before anything moves toward a sequence; here the critical review is a separate step you "must go find". For client filings under my signature, I would need the AI draft to be blocked from export until a qualified reviewer signs it off, not politely flagged.
answers.feedback: Keep: the guidance box, the audit-trail provenance, the checksum on saved files, the tooltip promising nothing saves without approval, and the gate flags on the status rail — those speak my language. Change: (1) make the post-save message visible on screen with a direct button to the review-vs-guidance check, not a hidden announcement pointing to another mode; (2) fix the misconfiguration message that references an "Author" button "below" that isn't below — that's the kind of sloppiness that erodes confidence in a compliance tool; (3) give me an admin setting to require reviewer sign-off on AI-assisted drafts before they count toward "required sections complete"; and (4) that placeholder example with sponsor contact details makes me ask where the chat data goes — I need a plain statement on data residency and whether client information trains anything.
answers.adoption: I'd pilot it on an internal mock dossier only. Team-wide adoption would require enforced review gates on AI drafts, a clear data-handling statement, and evidence the audit trail satisfies a client or Health Canada records request — until then it stays out of live client work.

answers.ease: On paper this looks manageable — the right-rail cards with a pass/fail badge and readiness flags for Documents, Fee and Valid eCTD mirror what I look for in docuBridge output, so my team would orient quickly. My worry is density: module tabs, a section tree, chips everywhere — my newer associates would need a proper SOP and training session before I let them near a live sequence.
answers.clarity: The vocabulary is right — sequences, leaf counts, purpose chips like "Response" and "Annual notification", CA-E/CA-W rule codes — that's our language, and I appreciate that. What is not clear is whether these "validation-rule-style IDs" are the actual Health Canada eCTD validation rules or the vendor's own approximation of them; "style" is doing a lot of work in that footnote and I'd need that answered before training anyone.
answers.trust: Not as it stands. Two things are disqualifying for a real filing: the export proceeding silently with no check when the validator is offline — that is exactly how a screening rejection ends up on my desk — and "Export anyway" being a mere browser confirm dialog with no audit trail of who accepted it. In a CRO, client filings need a documented QC gate, not a click-through.
answers.feedback: I genuinely like the re-run of validation on export and the explicit warning that screening would reject the package — that's more honest than some tools I've paid six figures for. Change three things: block or loudly flag exports when the validator is offline, never silent; make the "Export anyway" override a logged, reason-required action tied to a named user; and publish a mapping of the CA-E/CA-W codes to the official Health Canada validation rules with a version date, because those rules change and I need to know which set I'm being checked against. The truncated error list ("Show all 12 errors") is fine on screen, but give me an exportable full validation report I can attach to the submission file.

answers.ease: For me personally, the layout reads like something my team could pick up quickly — the module tabs M1–M5 and a section tree on the left mirror how we already think about eCTD structure in docuBridge. My one hesitation is the sheer number of chips and cards on one screen; I would want a half-day walkthrough before letting junior staff loose on the sequence controls, because "Make active" is a button you can click wrong.
answers.clarity: The terminology is genuinely the right terminology — sequences, leaves, lifecycle legality, XML backbone — this was clearly written by someone who has seen a Health Canada validation report. What I would want spelled out is the difference between the pre-computed structural check and the "Run full check (PDF conformance)" button; if my coordinator sees PASSED before running the full check, she may believe she's done when she isn't.
answers.trust: Not yet, and the walkthrough itself tells me why: if the validator is offline, the export proceeds silently with no check at all. That is exactly the kind of failure mode that gets a client filing screened out, and I would be the one on the phone explaining it. I also can't rely on "CA-E-style" rule IDs unless someone shows me they map to the actual current Health Canada validation rules version — we validate against LORENZ eValidator today and I'd need a side-by-side before signing off.
answers.feedback: I like the re-run of validation on export and the confirm dialog that says plainly Health Canada screening would reject the package — that's honest and it's more than some tools do. Concrete changes: the silent export when the validator is offline must become a hard block or at minimum a loud warning banner; the "Export anyway for internal review" package should be watermarked or named so it cannot be mistaken for a filing copy; and give me an exportable validation report (PDF/Excel) with all findings, not a truncated on-screen list, because I need to attach that to our QC record and circulate it to the client.

answers.ease: For me personally, the Portfolio page looks manageable — it's essentially the Excel tracker my team maintains by hand, with the module tower and fee status in one view. The Correspondence page is busier: three stacked panels behind a dossier lookup is the kind of thing I'd need to walk my coordinators through once or twice before they'd use it confidently.
answers.clarity: The regulatory vocabulary is correct, which I notice immediately — SAL, SDN, NOC, NOD, NON, Form V, NOA, the 45-day window and 24-month stay are all real Health Canada concepts used properly, and the "Screening vs Review decisions" hint is genuinely helpful for junior staff. The DIN hint ("Issued by Health Canada at NOC — leave blank until then") is exactly the guidance people get wrong. What "Start lifecycle" means, though, is unclear to me — I don't know what I'm starting or whether it has consequences.
answers.trust: Partially. The annual notification checklist recording who signed and when, with an audit event stream, is the right instinct — that's the kind of attributable record I need for client audits, and I appreciate the honesty that filings still happen with Health Canada. But litigation clocks like the 45-day action window and 24-month stay carry real legal exposure; I would not rely on a day-counter in a web tool without knowing exactly which date it's counting from and having our IP counsel verify it. For deadlines of that severity I'd keep our own tracker running in parallel for at least a year.
answers.feedback: I like the CSV client status report — I send exactly that to sponsors monthly and today it's assembled by hand — and the signed, timestamped checklist ticks are a genuine improvement over anything I've seen at this level. Concerns: the NOA clock ("12d for brand to act") needs to show its source date and calculation basis on hover, or my team will not trust it; correspondence records need document attachment, because a log entry without the actual HC letter behind it is half a record; and I'd want to know how any of this reconciles with what we already hold in Veeva Vault before I'd ask nine people to double-enter data.

answers.ease: For me personally, the Portfolio page looks manageable — cards, chips, an "Open" link, that's not far off what I see in Vault. But I'd have to train nine people on three separate pages (Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence) that each behave a bit differently, and the Correspondence page asking me to type a dossier ID and press "Open" feels like extra clicks compared to just landing on the right dossier from the portfolio row.
answers.clarity: The regulatory vocabulary is genuinely correct — SAL, SDN, NOC, NOD, NON, Form V, the 45-day window and 24-month stay — someone knew the Food and Drug Regulations and PM(NOC) Regulations when they wrote this. answers.trust: Partially. The annual notification checklist recording who signed and when on an audit event stream is exactly the kind of attribution I need for client accountability, and I appreciate the honesty of "the filings themselves still happen with Health Canada." But I would not run PM(NOC) litigation clocks — a 45-day s.6 window or a 24-month stay — off a day-counter in a web tool without knowing precisely what date it's counting from; those deadlines end careers if you get them wrong, and mine live in counsel-verified trackers today.
answers.feedback: I like the CSV client status report — I build that manually in Excel every month for sponsors, so that alone gets my attention — and the DIN hint "leave blank until NOC" will save my juniors real confusion. What I'd change: the correspondence hub only shows manually logged records, so it's a shadow register that drifts from reality unless someone is disciplined about entry — I'd want mandatory fields and a way to attach the actual HC letter, not just a log line. And the "NOA: 12d for brand to act" chip needs to show its source dates on hover, because I will not act on a bare number.

answers.ease: For me personally, the guided step rail with a saved session would be manageable — I don't have time to fight new software, and "resume where you left off" matters when I'm juggling twelve client files. The M1–M5 tabs with pass/todo markers map onto how my team already thinks in eCTD terms, so the learning curve looks reasonable. The 3D "submission tower" I could do without; I need a checklist, not a visualization.

"Ready to file" is a strong claim and I'd need to know exactly what it's asserting.
answers.trust: Not yet, not without seeing the validation engine behind that readiness chip — my name is on the client's cover letter, so I'd run everything through LORENZ docuBridge validation regardless. That said, the Account & security page saying self-hosted, API-enforced workspace scoping, and an append-only audit stream — and honestly admitting no SAML yet — is the most credible security write-up I've seen from a new vendor, and it's the sort of thing our IT and client auditors would actually accept.
answers.adoption: Cautiously possible as a supplementary tool, not a Vault replacement — we have too much invested in Veeva and clients contractually expect it. No SSO is a real blocker for a 400-person CRO's IT policy, and I'd want references from other Canadian sponsors before piloting. I could see trialing it with one or two smaller ANDS clients if a pilot goes well.
answers.feedback: I like the honest limitations on the security page, the correct dossier ID validation with CESG context, the placeholder-ID escape hatch, and auto-saved progress — all practical. Dislikes: the "Start over" button next to the readiness chip frightens me — one misclick on a 70%-ready client file is a disaster, so it needs a hard confirmation; rename or soften "Ready to file" unless it's backed by a published validation rule set I can show a client; drop or make optional the 3D tower; and add SSO and role-based permissions before any team of nine can use it, because I need to control who can touch which client's dossier.

answers.ease: For me personally, this looks manageable — the step rail and guided journey are closer to a TurboTax model than what we get from LORENZ, and my junior associates would probably ramp up quickly. My worry is the reverse: for people like me who already know the process, all the hand-holding and the "3D submission tower" could get in the way once you're on your fifth sequence of the day.
answers.clarity: The language is unusually clear for regulatory software — the dossier ID helper text explaining the REP request through CESG is exactly the kind of detail vendors normally get wrong. answers.feedback: I genuinely like the honest limits disclosure, the placeholder draft dossier ID for teams waiting on their REP request, and autosave with resumable sessions — those reflect real workflow.
